 El Niño explained: Why 43 counties will receive more rain than usual in new weather forecast
 Tuesday 10th November, 2026 08:29 AM | 
 By David Nthua 
 A wider shot of a flooded Nairobi CBD 
 Forty-three Kenyan counties are expected to receive more rainfall than usual during the October-December 2026 season, with meteorologists warning that some areas could experience heavy downpours, flooding and other weather-related challenges.
 The Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA), in a seasonal forecast for November-December, attributed the expected rainfall patterns partly to El Niño, a climate phenomenon involving the unusual warming of ocean waters in the Pacific Ocean.
 The warming thousands of kilometres away can influence weather conditions in different parts of the world, including rainfall patterns in Kenya.
 Why El Niño could bring more rain to Kenya
 El Niño is not rainfall itself. It is a climate phenomenon that develops when surface waters in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm.
 This warming affects the movement of air and clouds around the world, changing where and how much rainfall occurs.
 According to KMSA, the October-December rainfall season is influenced by several climate factors, including the movement of the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), which moves southwards during this period.
 The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), another climate pattern, also influences the amount and duration of rainfall. The authority explains that a positive IOD enhances rainfall, while El Niño can further increase rainfall when the two phenomena occur together.
 State of roads in Kitengela town following the past heavy rains. PHOTO/Christine Musa 
 This combination makes the ongoing rainy season important because the October-December period contributes more than 30 per cent of annual rainfall in several Kenyan counties.
 However, El Niño does not mean every part of Kenya will experience similar rainfall or flooding.
 Is your county among the 43 expecting more rain?
 KMSA has identified 43 counties where above-average rainfall is expected during the October-November-December season.
 They include Baringo, Bomet, Bungoma, Busia, Elgeyo-Marakwet, Embu, Garissa, Homa Bay, Isiolo, Kajiado, Kakamega, Kericho, Kiambu, Kilifi, Kirinyaga, Kisii, Kisumu, Kitui, Kwale, Laikipia, Lamu, Machakos, Makueni, Mandera, Meru, Migori, Mombasa, Murang’a, Nairobi, Nakuru, Nandi, Narok, Nyamira, Nyandarua, Nyeri, Siaya, Taita Taveta, Tana River, Tharaka-Nithi, Trans Nzoia, Uasin Gishu, Vihiga and Wajir.
 The forecast also indicates that much of West Pokot, Samburu and Marsabit could receive above-average rainfall, while Turkana and a few parts of the three counties are expected to experience near-average to above-average rainfall.
 Above-average rainfall means the expected amount is more than 125 per cent of the long-term average for the season. It does not mean that it will rain every day.
 KMSA warns that heavy rainfall events could occur in several parts of the listed counties, raising the possibility of overflowing rivers, flash floods, landslides and damage to roads, homes and crops.
 The rains could also benefit farmers through improved soil moisture, longer growing seasons and increased water availability.
 A flooded road in Nairobi after heavy rains pounded the city. PHOTO/Martin Oduor 
 The authority has advised Kenyans to follow regular weather updates and county-specific forecasts as conditions change.
 The developing weather situation also raises questions about Kenya’s preparedness for the expected El Niño rains , particularly in flood-prone areas.
 Residents in urban centres can also learn from recent flooding in Nairobi’s Parklands area , which highlighted concerns about drainage and preparedness.
